title: A dashboard to read the acquisition nights

html:
In Texas, the telescope works on its own all night. The equipment mostly belongs to Renaud Venne-Landry; I take care of acquisition and automation. In the morning, the question is always the same: how did the night go? The Voyager logs contain the whole answer, but in the form of tens of thousands of lines of text. Hence this dashboard, built to read them automatically.

Where the data comes from

Every morning, the night's files arrive from Texas on a small server at home. An ingestion program analyzes them and stores everything in a database:

  • the Voyager logs: exposures, focus runs, slews, errors, scheduler decisions;
  • the PHD2 guiding logs, guide frame by guide frame;
  • the image headers and a measurement made on each image: star size, sky background, star count;
  • the weather and the all-sky camera images.

The interface is a web application, available from any computer in the house. A menu switches from one site to another: Texas, home, and a mobile setup.

A score out of 100 for each night

To compare nights at a glance, each one gets a score out of 100, made of four equal parts:

  • star sharpness (mean HFD): 25 points at 2 pixels or less, none at 4 pixels;
  • guiding (RMS error): the lower the error, the higher the score;
  • efficiency: the share of the night actually spent exposing;
  • critical errors: each one costs points, and five are enough to empty this part.

In the calendar, the good nights stand out in blue, with the number of targets, exposures and hours, the Moon phase and a thin strip of sky images at the bottom of each cell.

A night under the magnifying glass

The night view is the one consulted most often. The main chart shows star size exposure after exposure, colored by filter. It tells the whole story of the night: the focus runs (green triangles), the meridian flip, the rejected exposures (circled in red), and the fact that OIII gives noticeably sharper stars here than Ha and SII.

Other tabs detail guiding quality, pointing, weather conditions, all-sky images, errors and scheduler decisions.

Where the night time goes

This is the most instructive page. Since August 2025, the shutter has been open for 68% of the available night time. The rest breaks down as follows:

Where the time goesHoursShare
Shutter open1,73468.3%
Moon with no possible target28311.2%
Site judged unsafe (weather)1957.7%
Other idle time1787.0%
Technical overhead1495.9%

If you remove the hours when the site was closed because of weather, efficiency rises to 74%. The best night reached 94.7%. The most surprising figure is the Moon's: more than 280 hours lost for lack of a target compatible with it. Hence the value of always keeping narrowband projects in the list.

Project progress

The scheduler page takes the RoboTarget targets and shows where each one stands: hours acquired per filter, hours remaining, priority and constraints. All the projects together are 74% complete. This is where the next additions are decided, and where it shows which targets have never been photographed.

Understanding the errors

Every warning and error in the logs is sorted by category: guiding, focus, pointing, external script, and so on. A timeline places them within the night. This is the page that showed that connection failures to the guiding software kept coming back, which led to a change in the script.

Another page tracks pointing: more than 7,200 plate solves over 184 nights, with a median offset under 2 arcseconds.

The sky, as seen by a machine

The site's all-sky camera takes an image at regular intervals. The dashboard turns this into a movie of the night and a strip summarizing the state of the sky hour by hour. A small neural network classifies each image: clear sky, partly cloudy, overcast. It is its answer that the script queries before opening a session.

This classification is still far from reliable. Hence the annotation tool, where the state of the sky is entered by hand, sector by sector. So far only 138 images out of more than 15,000 have been labelled: that is the work in progress.

What it changes

Before, a bad night remained a mystery, or took an hour of reading logs. Now a minute is enough to know whether the night was good, why it wasn't, and what is left to do on each project. And above all, recurring problems end up showing, whereas an isolated incident gets forgotten.
